\chapter{Background}
Printing in East Asia began with carved wooden blocks.
By the seventh century, Buddhist texts circulated in woodblock editions.
The Diamond Sutra of 868 is the earliest dated printed book.
Woodblock printing suited the logographic script well.
A single carved block could serve for decades of reprints.
Workshops in Chengdu and Hangzhou became early centers of the trade.
Officials used woodblock printing to standardize the Confucian classics.
Private publishers followed with almanacs, primers, and fiction.
By the eleventh century, woodblock printing supported a commercial book market.
Merchants sold popular titles from stalls at temple fairs.
Collectors prized fine impressions from carefully seasoned blocks.
Paper quality varied widely across regions and workshops.
Red ink marked imperial editions and celebratory printings.
The trade linked rural paper mills to urban bookshops.
The craft demanded close coordination between carvers, printers, and sellers.

\chapter{The Carver's Craft}
Pear wood and jujube wood were the preferred materials for blocks.
Carvers soaked the boards and planed them to a mirror finish.
In carved block printing, the text is first written on thin paper.
The sheet is pasted face down on the block for the carver to follow.
A skilled carver could finish a page of carved block printing in two days.
Fine lines demanded a steady hand and sharp knives.
Ink was ground fresh each morning and mixed to a thin consistency.
Mistakes were corrected by plugging the block with fresh wood.
Workshops guarded their carved block printing techniques as trade secrets.
Apprentices spent years learning to cut characters cleanly.
The finished blocks were brushed with ink and pressed against paper.
Each impression was checked for missing strokes before drying.
